section_summary: This section traces Japanese merchant shipping from the 1931 Chinese boycott and sterling crisis through fleet expansion, route competition, and the 1936 Shipping Route Control Law. It includes consular reports, file notes, trade statistics, a substantial report with translated Japanese legislation, and later records concerning wartime shipping and vessels in United States ports.

subfiles.title: Plight of shipowners in Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch on shipping losses caused by the Chinese boycott and sterling crisis.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 379, with a copy attached.

subfiles.title: Plight of shipowners
subfiles.about: Describes laid-up Japanese tonnage and proposed aid for shipowners.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese boycott and sterling depreciation depress freight and resale markets. Shipowners consider cooperative lay-ups, restrictions on foreign vessels, low-interest loans, and a gold embargo.

subfiles.title: Losses to Japanese shipping from the Manchurian incident
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on shipping losses during the Manchurian incident.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 404.

subfiles.title: Japanese shipping losses
subfiles.about: Gives estimates of Japanese ships laid up and losses attributed to the Manchurian incident.
subfiles.summary: Shippers estimate substantial losses and report about ten percent of vessels idle.

subfiles.title: Consent for publication of Italian diplomatic note
subfiles.about: Indexes a request for Italian consent to publish a 1918 ambassadorial note.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Instruction 542.

subfiles.title: Consent for publication of Japanese memorandum
subfiles.about: Indexes a request for Japanese consent to publish a 1918 government memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Instruction 222.

subfiles.title: Japanese shipping industry figures
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram with shipping statistics from Japan’s Department of Communications.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram 107, section H.

subfiles.title: Shipping statistics and conditions
subfiles.about: Reports company finances, fleet size, laid-up ships, and pressure from sterling depreciation and reduced China cargo.
subfiles.summary: Official figures list 914 large vessels and 356 vessels laid up in January 1932.

subfiles.title: Steamship earnings
subfiles.about: Indexes operating losses at Japan’s two largest steamship companies.
subfiles.summary: Nippon Yusen and Osaka Shosen passed dividends after losses during the boycott.

subfiles.title: Effects of the Chinese boycott on Japan
subfiles.about: Estimates the boycott’s effects on Japanese trade, industry, shipping, and investment in China.
subfiles.summary: Grew cautions that the depression and exchange-rate changes make precise attribution difficult, then estimates roughly $75 million in lost foreign trade through mid-1932. Cotton textiles, sugar refining, China-bound cargoes, and Japanese mills near Shanghai suffered; some carrying trade recovered after the Shanghai armistice. Tables compare 1930–1932 exports and imports for China and markets with substantial Chinese-controlled trade.

subfiles.title: Alleged merger of Nippon Yusen and Osaka Shosen
subfiles.about: Summarizes conflicting reports of a merger between Japan’s largest shipping interests.
subfiles.summary: Notes Osaka Shosen denials and apparent Nippon Yusen interest.

subfiles.title: Alleged merger of the Nippon Yusen Kaisha and the Osaka Shosen Kaisha
subfiles.about: Reports press claims and denials concerning a merger of two major Japanese shipping companies.
subfiles.summary: Garrels gives the reported fleet, route, and management terms while stressing that no agreement is confirmed. He considers possible effects on American shipping.

subfiles.title: White Star liners sold for Japanese shipbreaking
subfiles.about: Indexes a denial that purchased liners Gigantic and Baltic would become troopships.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 688.

subfiles.title: Sale of British ships to Japanese breakers
subfiles.about: Discusses the sale of old British ships and a denial that they would serve as troopships.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese consulate in Liverpool denies troopship rumors; a British official says the vessels were sold for breaking up.

subfiles.title: Projected growth in Japanese merchant shipping
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on new ships and shifts toward trans-Pacific and American routes.
subfiles.summary: Notes expansion despite declining Japanese activity in European waters.

subfiles.title: New Japanese cargo vessels for the New York route
subfiles.about: Reports planned diesel cargo ships for Nippon Yusen and Kokusai Kisen’s Orient–New York services.
subfiles.summary: Japanese shipping grows on American routes while declining in Europe.

subfiles.title: Sale of Albertic to Japanese shipbreakers
subfiles.about: Indexes the sale of the Cunard–White Star liner Albertic for breaking up.
subfiles.summary: Records an approximately £34,000 sale price.

subfiles.title: Japanese sailings between Brazil and Gulf ports
subfiles.from: Allen, Mississippi Valley Association, St. Louis
subfiles.about: Indexes concerns that Brazilian coffee cargoes support Japanese ships competing with Brazilian and American lines.
subfiles.summary: Coffee return cargoes enable direct Japanese sailings to Brazil.

subfiles.title: Japanese shipping policy
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch concerning Japanese shipping policy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 1149.

subfiles.title: Dutch East Indies concerns about Japanese shipping
subfiles.about: Indexes commentary on a possible ocean shipping agreement and Hart’s visit to China.
subfiles.summary: Suggests pressure for stronger Japanese government control of steamship companies.

subfiles.title: Possible Japanese steamship calls at Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Indexes Nippon Yusen’s inquiry into adding Guayaquil as a port of call.
subfiles.summary: Links the proposed call to Japanese trade with Ecuador.

subfiles.title: World tanker tonnage and Norwegian shipping
subfiles.about: Indexes information on tanker construction and Norwegian shipping interests.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 191.

subfiles.title: Plan to expand Japan’s merchant marine
subfiles.about: Indexes a reported plan to increase Japan’s fleet from four to six million tons.
subfiles.summary: Cites the Osaka Mainichi and a proposed Diet bill.

subfiles.title: Shipping expansion proposal
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed government bill to expand Japanese merchant tonnage.
subfiles.summary: The Ministry of Communications reportedly seeks a six-million-ton fleet.

subfiles.title: Japanese Shipping Route Control Law
subfiles.about: Analyzes the impending route-control law against subsidized shipbuilding and growing competition.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that Japan’s subsidized scrap-and-build program has produced modern vessels faster than established routes can absorb them. It surveys services and new ships between Japan and the United States, especially via Panama, and describes competition among major and smaller Japanese lines. It also assesses vessel quality and lists confidential industry sources.

subfiles.title: Shipping Route Control Law, Law No. 35
subfiles.about: Sets government powers to regulate Japanese shipping routes, competition, rates, reporting, and penalties.
subfiles.summary: The law permits advice, ordered route agreements, restrictions, and intervention in rates considered contrary to public benefit. It establishes reporting and inspection duties, a Shipping Route Control Committee, and fines for violations. Pages 56–58 contain an English translation; page 59 reproduces the Japanese text.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 177
subfiles.about: Defines coastal routes covered by the Shipping Route Control Law.
subfiles.summary: Includes Korea, Hokkaido, Sakhalin, and subsidized coastal services.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 178
subfiles.about: Establishes the Shipping Route Control Committee’s organization and duties.
subfiles.summary: The communications minister chairs a committee of up to fifteen members. It reviews route-control matters, although military or diplomatic secrecy may allow orders without committee review.

subfiles.title: Department of Communications Ordinance No. 23
subfiles.about: Prescribes shipping-company reports on routes, vessels, voyages, agreements, and business operations.
subfiles.summary: Companies must give advance notice of route changes and report operating details, agreements, capital, and fleet information to the communications ministry.

subfiles.title: Japanese texts of route-control ordinances
subfiles.about: Reproduces the Japanese originals of the route-control implementing ordinances.
subfiles.summary: Original texts accompany the English translations.

subfiles.title: Arrival of Canberra Maru at Tsingtao
subfiles.doc_type: document file note with despatch extract
subfiles.about: Reports a fast Osaka Shosen vessel arriving with Australian wheat.
subfiles.summary: Treats the Canberra Maru as evidence of Japanese maritime growth.

subfiles.title: Law for the Control of Sea Routes
subfiles.about: Refers the Department to the Yokohama consulate’s report and translation of the route-control law.
subfiles.summary: The embassy declines to send a duplicate translation because the consulate has supplied one.

subfiles.title: New Japanese express cargo vessel at Singapore
subfiles.about: Indexes Nippon Yusen’s new Akagi Maru service from Singapore to Northern Europe.
subfiles.summary: Notes continued expansion despite local opposition.

subfiles.title: Japanese express freight service from Malaya
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on Japanese services to Europe and the United States.
subfiles.summary: Mentions Osaka Shosen’s reported controlling interest in Kokusai Kisen.

subfiles.title: Japanese shipping and the rubber trade
subfiles.about: Discusses Japanese express freight capacity and rubber freight rates from Malaya.
subfiles.summary: A reported Osaka Shosen interest in Kokusai Kisen would strengthen Japanese service. The report attributes a temporary decline in Japanese rubber carriage to lower rates, with recovery expected after a rate increase.

subfiles.title: Shipping in Japan, March 1937
subfiles.about: Indexes plans to put Japanese shipbuilding on a semi-wartime footing.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 2368.

subfiles.title: Semi-wartime shipbuilding controls
subfiles.about: Reports proposed shipbuilding control and possible Navy purchase of Kawasaki Dockyards.
subfiles.summary: Also notes a rumored Nippon Yusen absorption of Kawasaki Kisen.

subfiles.title: Passenger-booking cancellations during the Sino-Japanese conflict
subfiles.about: Indexes suspected troop transport aboard two ships following cancellation of passenger bookings.
subfiles.summary: Also refers to conditions around Nagasaki.

subfiles.title: Disposition of former American steamships
subfiles.about: Indexes the sale of Tashmoo, Fort Armstrong, and Buffalo Bridge to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 212.

subfiles.title: Estimate of Japanese ships in United States ports
subfiles.about: Estimates the number of Japanese ships present in United States ports.
subfiles.summary: Commerce estimates twenty to thirty at any time using 1936 figures.

subfiles.title: Reported bomb threat against a Japanese ship at Seattle
subfiles.about: Records interdepartmental calls concerning a reported attempt to bomb a Japanese ship in Seattle.
subfiles.summary: State officials ask whether Justice has been informed and advise against publicity. Treasury later seeks State’s guidance because of the diplomatic implications.
